before: There is a code of manners, she knew, and its seventh article (possibly) states that on occasions like this one it falls to the woman, whatever her own work may be, to come to the aid of the young man across from her, so that he can bring out and ease the thighbones and ribs of his vanity, his pressing need to assert himself. Just as it is men’s duty, she thought, with her old-maidish sense of fair play, to help us if, for instance, the Underground caught fire. In that case, she thought, I’d certainly expect Mr. Tansley to get me out. But what if, she wondered, neither of us did either? So she sat there, smiling.

before: Nothing stirred in the drawing room or the dining-room or on the staircase. Only, through the rusty hinges and the swollen, sea-damp woodwork, certain breaths of air, broken off from the body of the wind (the house was ramshackle, after all), crept around corners and ventured indoors. You could almost imagine them, as they came into the drawing room, questioning and wondering, playing with the loose flap of hanging wallpaper, asking: would it hang much longer, when would it fall? Then, smoothly brushing the walls, they passed on thoughtfully, as if asking the red and yellow roses on the wallpaper whether they would fade, and questioning (gently, for they had time to spare) the torn letters in the wastepaper basket, the flowers, the books, all of which were now open to them—asking, Were they allies? Were they enemies? How long would they last?

before: Then, truly, peace had come. From the sea to the shore came breaths of peace, messages of it: never again to disturb its sleep, but to lull it into a deeper rest, and to confirm whatever the dreamers dreamed, in holiness and wisdom—what else could it be murmuring?—as Lily Briscoe laid her head on the pillow in the clean, quiet room and listened to the sea. In through the open window came the voice of the world’s beauty, murmuring too softly for its exact words to be made out—but what did that matter, if the meaning was clear? It pleaded with the sleepers (the house was full once more; Mrs. Beckwith was staying, and Mr. Carmichael as well) that if they would not actually come down to the beach, they should at least raise the blind and look out. Then they would see night flowing down in purple, his head crowned, his scepter set with jewels, and how a child might gaze into his eyes. And if they still held back (Lily, worn out by the journey, fell asleep almost at once, but Mr. Carmichael read a book by candlelight)—if they still refused, saying that this splendor of his was mere vapor, that the dew was stronger than he was, and that they would rather sleep—then the voice would sing its song gently, without complaint or argument. The waves would break gently (Lily heard them as she slept); the light fell tenderly (it seemed to come to her through her eyelids). And it all looked, thought Mr. Carmichael, closing his book and drifting off, very much the way it had looked years ago.
